The result builds on recent work exploring hybrid quantum‑classical learning architectures and suggests a near‑term pathway for quant firms to experiment with NISQ hardware, though the advantage remains task‑specific and does not yet constitute a universal quantum speedup.

FirstQFM, in collaboration with SW7 Group and Rigetti Computing, has successfully demonstrated a financial forecasting pilot using quantum reservoir computing (QRC) on Rigetti’s 108-qubit processor. This QRC system outperformed classical machine learning models and time-series foundation models in financial benchmarks, achieving significantly higher cumulative gross profit and loss and Sharpe ratios. The study highlights QRC as a promising and latency-efficient approach for deploying NISQ processors in quantitative finance, despite not claiming general quantum advantage. item.title: Quantum channel tomography: optimal bounds in the near-boundary regime
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article finally closes the last open case in quantum channel tomography by pinning down the query complexity when the dilation rate τ is just above one, a regime that had resisted analysis despite its relevance to near‑optimal process learning. By showing that diamond‑norm tomography loses Heisenberg scaling abruptly while Choi‑trace‑norm tomography degrades smoothly, the work clarifies how resource requirements transition from quantum‑enhanced to classical limits—a nuance that will guide experimental designs for characterising noisy intermediate‑scale devices. The tight lower and upper bounds also provide a benchmark for future algorithmic improvements, confirming that any further speed‑up must come from exploiting additional structure beyond low Kraus rank.

Quantum channel tomography (also known as quantum process tomography) is a fundamental task in quantum information and quantum computing, aiming to learn the full description of an unknown quantum channel from black-box queries. For channels with input dimension $d_1$, output dimension $d_2$, and Kraus rank at most $r$, [CGO+26] identifies the dilation rate $τ=rd_2/d_1\geq 1$ as a key parameter governing a Heisenberg-to-classical transition in query complexity. While the optimal bounds in the boundary regime ($τ=1$) and the away-from-boundary regime ($τ\geq 1+Ω(1)$) are now known, the precise behavior in the near-boundary regime ($1<τ<1+o(1)$) has remained unresolved. In this paper, we close this gap, thereby fully settling the query complexity of quantum channel tomography. Specifically, we show that the query complexity is - $Ω(rd_1d_2/\varepsilon^2)$ for diamond norm error $\varepsilon$, matching the upper bound by [MB26, CGO+26], - $Θ(d_1^2/\varepsilon+\min\{(τ-1)d_1^2,(τ-1)^2d_1^2d_2^2\}/\varepsilon^2)$ for Choi trace norm error $\varepsilon$. Our results reveal two qualitatively different forms of the Heisenberg-to-classical transition. For diamond norm tomography, the Heisenberg scaling disappears suddenly as soon as $τ$ leaves the boundary regime. In contrast, Choi trace norm tomography exhibits a gradual transition from Heisenberg to classical scaling as $τ$ moves from the boundary regime to the away-from-boundary regime.

item.title: Unifying entanglement and nonclassicality via the Narcowich-Wigner spectrum
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the Narcowich‑Wigner spectrum can serve as a universal bridge between single‑mode nonclassicality and multipartite entanglement, extending the well‑known two‑mode mixing connection to arbitrary multimode Gaussian dynamics. By turning phase‑space negativity into a practical sufficient condition for NPT entanglement, the authors provide a compact, experimentally friendly way to certify complex entanglement structures using only single‑mode measurements—a tool that could streamline benchmarking of continuous‑variable processors and error‑correction codes. The work not only tightens existing criteria but also opens a new analytical avenue for probing bosonic resources across many platforms, though its applicability remains limited to Gaussian unitaries and may need adaptation for non‑Gaussian operations.

Entanglement and nonclassicality are two fundamental features of quantum mechanics which serve as resources in quantum information processing tasks and are tightly connected by two-mode mixing. In this work, we show that the connection between entanglement and nonclassicality extends well beyond the two-mode mixing setting by considering the case of arbitrary multimode Gaussian evolutions. Using the Narcowich-Wigner spectrum as our main technical tool to quantify single-mode phase-space nonclassicality, we derive sufficient conditions for a single-mode state to generate NPT entanglement after a multimode Gaussian unitary evolution, which both tighten and generalize existing criteria. As an application, we obtain simple single-mode protocols for quantitatively testing the entanglement structure of multimode quantum states over arbitrary bipartitions. Our results identify the Narcowich-Wigner spectrum as a powerful tool for investigating fundamental properties of bosonic quantum states.

item.title: Agentic Pipelines for Mapping Topological Codes to Quantum Hardware
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it delivers the first formally verified (Lean‑proved) workflow that guarantees a topological error‑correcting code’s low‑energy subspace survives the messy translation from abstract Hamiltonian to real quantum hardware. By coupling AI agents with rigorous verification, the authors can pinpoint and bound unwanted interactions far more tightly than the traditional sum‑of‑strengths approach—crucial for designing devices that meet the stringent gap requirements of fault‑tolerant computing. The method also flags the most problematic qubits and couplings, giving hardware engineers concrete targets for improvement as the field races toward scalable, error‑corrected processors.

Mapping a prescribed many-body Hamiltonian to a particular quantum hardware is generally an approximate process, resulting in both intended and unwanted quantum dynamics. We introduce an AI-agent-assisted workflow that uses Lean to establish whether an effective device Hamiltonian retains the intended low-energy subspace of the target many-body Hamiltonian. We demonstrate this approach with topological quantum error correction (QEC), providing, to our knowledge, the first Lean-verified pipeline connecting a code space to low-energy states of a device model. Starting from qubits and parity checks, the pipeline constructs the ideal Hamiltonian whose lowest energy states form the intended code space, and determines the excitation gap that protects that code space. It then tests if the device retains the required number of isolated low-energy states and quantifies how closely their subspace matches the intended code space. We compare three bounds on unwanted energy shifts obtained by: summing the interaction strengths, grouping the anticommuting Pauli interactions, and diagonalizing the Hamiltonian. Pauli grouping yields a bound that is tighter than the conventional sum and closer to the diagonalization result, avoiding overly conservative compensation requirements. The workflow also identifies the strongest unwanted interactions and the qubits they affect, providing specific targets for improving device couplings and controls. We demonstrate our framework using an eight-qubit toric-code array on a superconducting device, where the same driven device generates both the required four-qubit interactions as well as unwanted dynamics. An AI agent identifies viable device parameters within a prescribed leakage budget, and Lean verifies four isolated low-energy states close to the ideal code space. Our workflow supports predictive hardware engineering for analog implementations of QEC codes.

item.title: Qyantram: A Transparent and Verifiable Quantum Computing Platform
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because QYANTRAM delivers the first openly traceable compilation pipeline that lets researchers see every routing decision and verify circuit transformations mathematically exactly—even on hardware‑scale layouts of up to 156 qubits. By exploiting idle |0⟩ qubits, the platform reduces verification complexity from exponential in total qubits to exponential only in the active subset, delivering millisecond‑level checks and a reported 10 000× speed‑up that could become a practical tool for rapid error‑identification and variational model debugging. The trade‑off is a modest increase (≈1.27×) in SWAP overhead compared with aggressive optimizers like SABRE, so users will need to balance transparency against raw circuit depth when targeting near‑term noisy devices.

Most quantum circuit platforms focus on idealized circuit assembly and simulation, hiding hardware compilation, error identification, and variational model training behind black-box operations. QYANTRAM addresses this gap through an open platform comprising four subsystems, built around evidence-backed results and independent verification. Its staged compilation pipeline makes every transformation traceable, while the router publishes rejected SWAP candidates and their scores for transparent decision-making. Verification exploits inactive qubits remaining in the |0> state, reducing complexity from 2^N to 2^k for k active qubits. This mathematically exact reduction enables full pre-compilation verification on 127- and 156-qubit layouts, achieving approximately 10,000x speed-ups with execution times below one millisecond. The error identification engine exhaustively evaluates all Pauli error patterns without sampling, matching closed-form predictions within 2.8e-17. Its machine-learning engine achieves numerical agreement within 2.0e-15 of qiskit.quantum_info while training 25-50 times faster. The router introduces approximately 1.27x more SWAP gates than Qiskit's SABRE due to its omission of optimization, trading routing efficiency for complete decision transparency and traceability.

item.title: Spin SYK-dot chains: entanglement bound and resource estimates towards a quantum advantage
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints the size regime where a spin‑SYK dot chain could finally outpace classical tensor‑network methods, showing that only dots with roughly 15–21 qubits would demand two‑qubit error rates near 10⁻⁶—well beyond current NISQ capabilities. By deriving an entanglement bound and concrete Trotter‑step costs, the authors connect SYK physics to realistic hardware requirements, offering a rare quantitative roadmap for quantum advantage in strongly correlated many‑body simulations. The work also validates its estimates with matrix‑product‑state and variational circuit benchmarks, highlighting that even modest inter‑dot coupling keeps entanglement low enough for classical compression up to about 40 qubits. Readers should note the stark gap between these theoretical thresholds and today’s error rates, underscoring both the promise of SYK models as a benchmark and the urgent need for error‑corrected platforms.

Ground states of Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK)-type models are volume-law entangled, which makes them costly both for tensor networks and for quantum hardware simulations. Thus, it remains unclear where quantum hardware could outperform classical simulation of such models. In this work, we study a spin SYK-dot chain, in which q dense SYK dots of p qubits are joined by single ZZ bonds of strength K. The entanglement across any cut is then bounded by floor(p/2) ln 2 plus the inter-dot entanglement, and the two-qubit depth of one Trotter step is set by p alone. A resource estimate shows that a quantum advantage for the ground state could appear only for dots of about 15 to 21 qubits or more. There, a single Trotter step already requires two-qubit error rates of order 10^{-6}, beyond the reach of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. We test the assumptions of this estimate with an imaginary-time matrix product state (MPS) that applies each dot as one block. It agrees with exact diagonalisation at (p, q) = (6, 2). At (5, 2), a variational circuit with the same dot-plus-link layout comes within 3.6% of the exact energy, and noisy simulations show that its fidelity decays as assumed in the resource estimate. At (8, 5), i.e., N = 40 qubits, the energy converges at bond dimension chi = 768, far below the exact value 2^20, and the inter-dot entanglement stays small and is set mainly by K. Out-of-time-order correlators across the links decay on a time scale that shrinks rapidly with |K|. Thus, the dot size p and the inter-dot coupling K together set the entanglement of the chain, and with it where a quantum advantage could appear.

item.title: Taming a macroscopic free mass through continuous quantum measurement
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first time a truly free‑mass system—a milligram‑scale rotor—has been tamed by continuous quantum measurement, pushing control into the ultra‑low‑frequency regime where environmental damping is only a few nanohertz. By achieving conditional states with effective temperatures near 140 nK, the work outperforms previous tabletop optomechanics by two orders of magnitude and opens a new platform for precision sensing, tests of collapse models, and probing quantum gravity effects at macroscopic scales. The breakthrough demonstrates that even without a confining potential, massive objects can be monitored with quantum‑limited precision, though scaling to larger masses will still require further advances in isolation and readout noise suppression.

The free particle is the most elementary dynamical system in quantum mechanics. Despite remarkable progress in quantum control of increasingly massive solid-state mechanical oscillators, the analogous control of the free-particle counterpart has remained elusive. Dissipation and environmental noise have prevented such control in the inherently low-frequency domain of free-particle dynamics---a regime of growing importance for quantum sensing and tests of fundamental physics. Here we realize a suspended 1-milligram rotor operating in the free-particle regime with exceptional environmental isolation. Combining this isolation with a low-noise measurement architecture, we directly resolve thermal fluctuations in the motion associated with a damping rate of only 7~nHz. Through continuous quantum measurement of the rotor, we localize its otherwise unconfined motion, obtaining conditional states with entropic temperatures as low as 140~nK as a quantitative measure of control in the free-particle regime. This is two orders of magnitude below temperatures previously achieved in tabletop optomechanical experiments. We demonstrate immediate utilities of the new operating regime, setting new constraints on modifications of quantum mechanics and benchmarking inferred entanglement-to-decoherence rate ratios nearly two orders of magnitude beyond the state of the art for tests of gravity at the quantum-classical interface.

item.title: eigenkit: A Provider-Neutral Quantum Computing Library
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it tackles a persistent bottleneck in quantum software: the friction of moving an algorithm between simulators and real devices with differing APIs and performance characteristics. By introducing eigenkit’s provider‑neutral circuit layer and unified gradient interface, the authors give researchers a practical way to benchmark and select the most suitable backend—something that recent multi‑provider frameworks have hinted at but not yet delivered at scale. The work underscores that portability is more than convenience; it can directly affect runtime efficiency and fidelity on hardware such as IBM’s Heron or IQM’s Emerald, though users must still consider topology matching and workload‑specific performance variations.

Quantum software ecosystems provide increasingly capable tools for simulation and hardware execution, but differences in programming models, supported features, and backend capabilities can make it difficult to move and systematically compare the same quantum algorithm across execution environments. We introduce eigenkit, a provider-neutral quantum computing library that separates algorithm definition from backend execution through a common circuit representation and provider interface. The library currently supports 12 execution providers spanning simulators and quantum hardware, provides backend-independent gradient computation, and integrates with standard scientific-computing and machine-learning workflows through NumPy, PyTorch, and scikit-learn interfaces. We evaluate the practical relevance of this abstraction across both simulation and quantum hardware. Simulator performance varies substantially with circuit size, structure, batching, and application workload, showing that no single backend is consistently preferable. On quantum hardware, experiments on IBM Heron and IQM Emerald show that which processor is better suited to a given algorithm depends not only on hardware constraints, but also on how well the topology of the quantum algorithm matches the physical connectivity of the processor. These results demonstrate that backend portability is not only a software-design convenience, but can be important for both computational efficiency and quantum execution quality.

item.title: Towards Optimal Routing Strategies for qLDPC codes on Silicon Spin Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a bottleneck for deploying high‑rate qLDPC error‑correction on silicon spin qubits by showing that the choice of shuttling strategy can dominate logical performance, with the optimal approach minimizing the longest travel distance rather than total distance. By comparing square and diagonal grids, the authors demonstrate that adding modest diagonal links can suppress logical error rates by up to two orders of magnitude—a result that directly informs future chip layout and control‑software design for scalable spin‑based processors. The work bridges recent theoretical advances in qLDPC codes with concrete hardware constraints, highlighting a practical pathway toward fault‑tolerant quantum memory on silicon.

One of the major challenges of implementing high-rate quantum error correction codes, like qLDPC codes, is realizing the required long-range interactions. Spin qubit platforms can provide this connectivity by shuttling qubits next to each other whenever they need to interact. When doing this, the performance of the code depends on the shuttling strategy. We study memory experiments of the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle (Gross) code on two shuttling grids for future spin qubit devices: a square grid and a square grid with diagonals. We compare three shuttling strategies, structured and random initial layouts, and a range of shuttling noise models spanning best- and worst-case scenarios. The best strategy minimizes the longest distance travelled rather than the total distance. The initial layout has only a weak effect, whereas adding diagonals to the grid reduces the logical error rate by up to two orders of magnitude which may have implications for future hardware design.

item.title: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article spotlights a concrete obstacle that has limited AI‑driven scientists from reliably reproducing quantum‑computing papers, revealing a mismatch between published methods and the information an autonomous agent can parse. By building OmniQ—a vetted platform that turns literature into executable tasks—and introducing Residual Agents that learn from human‑guided repairs, the authors demonstrate a measurable boost in reproducibility across simulation, algorithmic, and property‑characterization studies. The work signals a practical step toward scalable, AI‑assisted quantum research pipelines, while also underscoring that expert oversight remains essential until self‑improving agents can fully bridge the documentation gap.

AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. item.title: Entanglement inference from quantum erasure and path discrimination
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how to rigorously extract the minimum amount of multipartite entanglement that must have been present in an experiment solely from quantum‑eraser and path‑discrimination data, closing a long‑standing loophole where recovered interference fringes could be misleading. By providing exact semidefinite‐programming bounds and explicit state constructions for noisy GHZ preparations, the work links entanglement certification directly to observable measurement records—a capability that will tighten verification protocols for quantum sensors and near‑term processors. It also clarifies how additional parity or marker measurements can boost certification, offering a practical roadmap for experimental groups seeking device‑independent guarantees without assuming ideal sources. The results therefore sharpen both the theory and practice of entanglement witnessing in hardware‑focused quantum technologies.

Fringes recovered by conditioning on quantum-eraser outcomes do not, by themselves, establish entanglement. We determine the minimum entanglement compatible with recorded eraser data when the preparation may be mixed, distinguishing these data from independently determined optimal which-path distinguishabilities and additional joint measurement outcomes. For noisy Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) preparations, explicit compatible states establish sharp entanglement-depth thresholds and show how parity information strengthens certification. A matching converse establishes the exact threshold for two complete Pauli-outcome distributions. For an ideal three-qubit eraser, we classify the additional marker measurement directions that certify genuine multipartite entanglement within a fixed eraser configuration and determine the separate minima of compatible concurrence and squared GHZ fidelity for specified tilted axes. For noisy three-qubit data, an exact semidefinite characterization and constructive converse determine biseparable compatibility at arbitrary fixed local measurement axes, with rational certificates bounding one example. These results establish what entanglement is required by the measurement record, rather than inferred from assumptions about the source.

item.title: Quantum simulation of dissipative acoustic and elastic waves by Schrödingerisation: absorbing boundaries and explicit polynomial-size circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how to embed simple absorbing “sponge” layers into quantum simulations of acoustic and elastic waves by using Schrödingerisation, turning the inherently dissipative dynamics into a family of unitary circuits that require only one or two auxiliary qubits. By providing explicit polynomial‑size circuit constructions in one, two and three dimensions, it overcomes the closed‑system limitation of earlier wave‑equation simulators and opens the door to realistic modeling of seismic, materials‑science and other wave‑based problems on quantum hardware. The analysis predicts a constant success probability (≈0.4 × the remaining energy) and exact recovery on the truncated auxiliary axis, making the approach compatible with near‑term devices despite the need to manage controlled‑NOT overhead and truncation errors.

Explicit quantum circuits for the acoustic and elastic wave equations, obtained by Hamiltonian simulation of their first-order forms, conserve energy and therefore describe closed domains: an outgoing wave reflects off the edge of the computational region or, with periodic boundaries, wraps around and re-enters from the opposite side. We open the domain with the simplest physical absorber, a graded sponge layer in which every wave field is damped at a rate that grows towards the outer edge, and implement the resulting dissipative dynamics on a quantum simulator by Schrödingerisation, which turns a non-unitary linear evolution into a family of unitary ones by means of a single auxiliary variable. We derive the whole chain from the partial differential equation to the circuit, in one, two and three dimensions. An independent finite-difference solver confirms that damping all wave fields absorbs far better than the common velocity-only damping mask. For the sponge the quantum analysis is sharp: recovery is exact on the whole non- negative half of the auxiliary axis at every time; that axis can be truncated periodically at a length set by the largest damping rate and the simulated time; and the success probability is a fixed constant, about 0.4, times the fraction of the energy not yet absorbed, with only one or two auxiliary qubits measured. On the circuit side, the damping step, which generic synthesis compiles into a number of controlled-NOT gates exponential in the number of qubits, factorises exactly into polynomially many multi-controlled phase gates. Gate-level simulations on up to 25 qubits agree with the classical solutions of the damped wave equations.

item.title: MBUndo: Sound, Automatic, and Efficient Measurement-Based Uncomputation for Quantum Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces MBUndo, the first automated compiler pass that identifies where ancilla qubits can be safely measured and rewrites their unitary uncomputation into cheap phase‑correction operations, dramatically cutting the costly T‑gate overhead in generic quantum circuits. By extending measurement‑based uncomputation from hand‑crafted examples to any algorithmic design, it dovetails with recent hardware trends that make mid‑circuit measurements fast and reliable, opening a practical path for more efficient fault‑tolerant implementations of large‑scale algorithms such as Shor’s or quantum chemistry simulations. The approach does rely on the availability of low‑latency feed‑forward control, so its full benefit will be realized as those capabilities mature in next‑generation quantum processors.

Quantum programs that use temporary values, known as \emph{ancilla} qubits, must explicitly \emph{uncompute} each ancilla back to zero to ensure that the program produces correct outputs. Conventional uncomputation uses unitary quantum gates, whereas leading quantum algorithms now leverage \emph{measurement-based uncomputation} (MBU), which replaces costly unitary $T$ gates with cheaper measurements and phase corrections. Current quantum programming frameworks can use measurement to uncompute specific gates such as Toffoli. No automatic transformation, however, accepts an arbitrary circuit whose ancillas are computed and uncomputed via the standard approach and converts the circuit to use MBU\@. Researchers instead apply MBU to individual circuit designs by hand, which limits algorithm development and compiler optimization. Such a transformation has not existed due to two fundamental unknowns: where MBU applies and which gates realize MBU for an arbitrary computation. To solve these, we first present a static analysis that identifies, for each ancilla qubit, each circuit position where measurement is sound --- subsuming basic assumptions that MBU only applies at the end of a circuit. Next, we present circuit transformations that soundly turn unitary uncomputation gates into efficient phase corrections after measurement --- generalizing rewrite rules from prior literature that are either limited to a single gate or not applicable to a general circuit. We present \textsf{MBUndo}, an integrated compiler pass that automatically converts circuits to measurement-based uncomputation. It requires no user annotations other than which qubits are ancillas, the same as needed by existing uncomputation synthesizers, and can enhance their output circuits. We evaluate \textsf{MBUndo} on 22 benchmarks to reveal \emph{T} gate reductions of ${>}36.5\%$ over uncomputation synthesizers.

We show that topological edge states can be realized in a simple superconducting circuit composed of an inductively shunted flux qubit. The Josephson potential of that qubit forms a honeycomb lattice similar to the case of graphene. The additional shunting element produces a quartic potential along one flux direction, which effectively creates a boundary in flux space. We map analytically the low-energy dynamics of the circuit to an extended Su--Schrieffer--Heeger (SSH) chain, in which a quartic potential is added to the usual SSH Hamiltonian. This mapping is confirmed by numerical simulations of the full superconducting circuit. We argue that chiral symmetry still holds for the edge states of the extended model around a chiral point in parameter space. Close to this point, we numerically find that edge states in our superconducting circuit are topologically protected against perturbations that obey chiral symmetry, as is the case for charge noise. Our results show that topological effects previously thought to occur in multi-qubit systems, such as protection against decoherence, can also be found in much simpler single superconducting qubits.

Measurement-Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (MDI-QKD) enables secure communication without trusting the measurement devices, but its performance critically depends on the quality of the employed photon sources. We compare MDI-QKD implementations based on Weak Coherent Pulses (WCPs) with those employing Quantum Dot (QD) single-photon sources. WCP-based schemes are fundamentally limited by Poissonian photon-number statistics, imposing a trade-off between single- and multi-photon emissions, whereas QD sources exhibit sub-Poissonian statistics with low antibunching parameter $g^{(2)}(0)$. Using a decoy-state analysis for both source types, we find that even at moderate mean photon numbers, QD-based implementations outperform the best-case WCP configuration - where the mean photon number is optimised at each transmission distance - across the full range of transmission distances. We further incorporate the effect of imperfect photon indistinguishability via Hong-Ou-Mandel interference visibilities into the security framework and demonstrate that both source types are highly sensitive to even small deviations from ideal indistinguishability, significantly affecting achievable key rates and maximum transmission distance.

item.title: Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Classification: A Comparative Study with Classical Kernels
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that once measurement budgets, hyper‑parameter tuning and evaluation costs are rigorously controlled, quantum kernel classifiers offer no statistically significant accuracy boost over a well‑tuned classical RBF kernel on real‑world datasets. By treating the comparison itself as an experimental variable, the authors reveal that most of the observed performance gain comes from bandwidth tuning rather than any intrinsic quantum advantage, calling into question earlier benchmark claims that omitted these controls. The work underscores that near‑term quantum machine‑learning research must prioritize fair protocol design and hardware improvements before expecting practical superiority over classical methods.

Quantum kernel methods are the most concrete near-term proposal for quantum machine learning on classical data, yet published benchmarks disagree on whether they outperform tuned classical kernels, and the disagreement cannot be resolved from the literature because the comparisons are not protocol-controlled. We argue that the obstacle is one of measurement, not theory: the usual setup fixes the quantum feature map's data scaling while grid-searching the classical kernel's hyperparameters, recomputes nothing per fold, and reports cost in simulator time. We therefore treat the comparison itself as the object of study and impose three controls. The bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical $γ$, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations. On top of these we run a factorial design of 324 cells in which dimensionality, training size, class separability and data structure are explicit covariates, together with four standard datasets, a shots-versus-gate-noise ablation, and a cost sweep. The dominant effect we measure is not quantum: tuning the feature map's bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data, exceeding every quantum-classical difference we observe. Tuned quantum kernels are then statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on all four real datasets. The advantage on synthetic data is confined almost entirely to data generated by the feature map itself, and it shrinks with dimensionality (-0.0045 per qubit) while growing with sample size. Finite sampling costs an order of magnitude more accuracy than gate and readout noise, and a fidelity kernel needs $5\times10^{7}$ circuits at n = 10,000. Protocol variance is thus sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions.

item.title: Resource efficient Sample Based Quantum Simulation through Fragmentation and Virtual Partitioning of QPU
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a practical route to scaling quantum‑chemical simulations on today’s noisy devices by fragmenting the problem and virtually partitioning the QPU, cutting two‑qubit depth by up to half and slashing runtime by more than 80 % while still reaching chemical accuracy. By coupling a “half‑qubit” ansatz with an HCI expansion, the authors show that only a vanishing fraction of the determinant space needs to be sampled, enabling active spaces as large as 104 spin orbitals on 52 qubits—far beyond what prior sample‑based methods could handle. The work directly tackles the twin bottlenecks of circuit depth and classical post‑processing in quantum‑centric supercomputing, suggesting that near‑term hardware can now address chemically relevant systems such as drug‑target complexes.

Present-day sample-based quantum algorithms within quantum-centric supercomputing workflows require substantial classical post-processing, large circuit depths to produce chemically relevant samples, and long QPU times to execute the many circuits needed for molecules of chemically relevant size. We introduce FMO-QVM-HCI-HSQD, a resource-efficient sample-based framework that breaks a large problem into fragments, runs the fragments in parallel on virtual regions of the QPU, and reduces circuit depth through a half-qubit ansatz whose samples seed an HCI expansion. We demonstrate the algorithm on ibm_marrakesh and ibm_boston for the water trimer and the carmofur_Mpro complex with up to 52 qubits, benchmarking against FMO-CCSD(T), FMO-CASCI and FMO-HCI. For the water trimer (14 spin orbitals for monomers, 28 for dimers), our method reduces the two-qubit depth by 39% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD and the QPU time by 82% compared to sequential FMO-SQD, and accesses 3% of the determinant subspace versus 40% for FMO-SQD, while achieving more accurate energies. For the carmofur_Mpro complex (16 and 32 spin orbitals), it reduces the two-qubit depth by 47% and the QPU time by 20% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD, and accesses 0.007% of the determinant subspace versus 40%, while remaining within chemical accuracy. Extending the carmofur_Mpro active space in the 6-31G basis to 52 and 104 spin orbitals, sampled on 26 and 52 qubits, the total energy deviates from FMO-HCI by only 1.22 mHa. These results show that combining fragmentation, virtual QPU partitioning and half-qubit sampling makes sample-based quantum simulation of chemically relevant systems feasible on current hardware.

item.title: Control-Noise Trade-offs in Industrially Integrated ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ Spin-1/2 Qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that silicon‑spin qubits fabricated in a commercial 300 mm foundry can already achieve primitive gate fidelities of 99.99 % while displaying improved idle coherence and reduced device‑to‑device variability, demonstrating that industrial processes are no longer a barrier to high‑quality quantum hardware. The work also reveals a subtle control‑noise trade‑off: moving micromagnets farther from the quantum well—necessary for back‑end‑of‑line routing in dense two‑dimensional arrays— lowers magnetic gradients, which suppresses charge‑noise‑induced frequency jitter but weakens electrically driven spin resonance and makes drive errors more prominent at modest Rabi rates. These findings give foundries concrete design knobs to balance scalability with control performance as silicon spin qubits move toward fault‑tolerant architectures.

Scaling silicon spin qubits to fault-tolerant processors requires semiconductor foundry integration, yet it remains unclear how industrial fabrication and dense device integration affect qubit control and noise. Here we study ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ electron spin-1/2 qubits fabricated using Intel's industry-compatible 300 mm process and incorporating micromagnets for electrically driven spin resonance, using a high-performance device fabricated in the RIKEN research cleanroom as a reference. Primitive $π/2$-gate fidelities reach the 99.99% level in the Intel devices, which also exhibit longer idle coherence, weaker low-frequency correlations and reduced qubit-to-qubit variability across several measured characteristics. In the present Intel devices, the micromagnets are integrated inline with the back-end-of-line (BEOL) contact routing, with their separation from the quantum well set through the vertical stack design. Relative to the reference, their larger separation contributes to weaker longitudinal and transverse magnetic-field gradients. The weaker longitudinal gradient suppresses the conversion of charge noise into qubit-frequency fluctuations, whereas the weaker transverse gradient reduces electrically driven spin-resonance efficiency and makes drive-dependent errors relevant at lower Rabi frequencies. Additional BEOL routing and metal levels required for two-dimensional arrays make such placement decisions increasingly consequential when scaling. These results establish an integration-level control-noise trade-off linking micromagnet placement within densely routed layouts to achievable gate performance, while very high-fidelity operation remains possible in industrially fabricated devices.

item.title: Hybrid Quantum Algorithms for Trade Surveillance Analytics
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that hybrid quantum‑classical classifiers can already rival most conventional machine‑learning models on a realistic anti‑money‑laundering task, with the HQNN beating six of eight classical baselines and delivering competitive F1 scores even on noisy IBM hardware. By combining a tiny five‑qubit circuit with a classical network that sets every rotation angle, the authors demonstrate a practical route to leverage near‑term quantum devices for high‑dimensional financial analytics—a field where recent advances in quantum kernels and QNNs have struggled to scale. Although XGBoost still leads, the results suggest that hybrid approaches could soon narrow the gap between quantum prototypes and production‑grade fraud detection systems.

Anti-money laundering (AML) and trade surveillance remain largely manual: rule-based monitoring raises alerts of which, by estimate, over 95% are false positives, each reviewed by a human analyst. We benchmark four quantum and hybrid classifiers against classical baselines on a synthetic pump-and-dump detection task: a fidelity-based quantum k-nearest-neighbours classifier (QKNN) with clustering-based routing; a quantum support vector machine (QSVM) on a one-body projected quantum kernel; a 20-qubit quantum neural network (QNN) with a Pauli-ZZ feature map and RealAmplitudes ansatz; and a hybrid quantum neural network (HQNN) in which a small classical network generates every rotation angle of a five-qubit circuit. Baselines are logistic regression, XGBoost, one- and three-hidden-layer neural networks, and classical k-nearest neighbours. All models share one stratified split of 1000 accounts (800 train, 200 test, 20% suspicious) and two 20-feature representations (ANOVA and PCA); QKNN and QSVM are also tested under simulated noise, and the HQNN is run on the ibm_fez processor. The best model is classical XGBoost on ANOVA features, at a suspicious-class F1 of 61.4%. The HQNN is the strongest quantum-hybrid model, at 54.5-57.9% F1 on an ideal simulator and 55.4-59.8% on ibm_fez, ahead of six of eight classical configurations; at a 15% false-positive rate, half its alerts are genuinely suspicious. Versus the QNN (42.0% F1), it raises under half the false alarms at similar recall with a quarter of the qubits. The QKNN reaches 43.5% F1 (44.4% under noise), above classical KNN (35.6%); the QSVM does not exceed 41%. We observe no quantum advantage, but a five-qubit hybrid on today's noisy hardware already matches well-tuned classical models, with room to grow via richer circuits and larger devices. We contribute a like-for-like comparison with classical models on shared data, splits and features.

item.title: Engineered Learning Problems on Noisy Quantum Processors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks one of the few empirical demonstrations that a quantum‑enhanced machine‑learning model—specifically a projected quantum kernel—can outpace all tested classical classifiers on an engineered classification task using up to 45 noisy qubits, and it does so reproducibly across multiple superconducting processors. By showing how error‑mitigation techniques not only improve raw hardware fidelity but also raise the difficulty of the corresponding classical problem, the work highlights a concrete pathway for quantum advantage in near‑term QML despite the artificial nature of the benchmark. The authors caution that state‑of‑the‑art tensor‑network simulations still close much of the gap, underscoring that scaling to realistic data sets will be the next critical hurdle.

Despite quantum machine learning being an active topic of research, demonstrations of algorithms run on quantum hardware beating classical methods remain rare. In this work, we demonstrate a significant performance gap using a projected quantum kernel for $n=15,30$ and $45$ qubits over classical methods on an engineered classification problem, and show reproducibility of the results over different quantum processor units. We also demonstrate how error mitigation can widen this gap, both by improving hardware performance but also by increasing the classical difficulty, with different techniques contributing unequally to these phenomena. This work provides strong evidence that superior empirical performance of quantum hardware over all classical techniques is an achievable goal in quantum machine learning, albeit for an artificial problem. However, as with any application relying on observables, beating state-of-the-art simulation methods remains the primary challenge, as our matrix product state results here show.

item.title: Overcoming the Representational Limitations of Amplitude Encoding for Quantum Neural Networks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints a fundamental blind spot in amplitude‑encoded quantum neural networks: the unavoidable loss of information under uniform real scaling, which caps their expressive power regardless of circuit depth. By introducing a simple, parameter‑free nonlinear preprocessing step that restores sensitivity to all real inputs while preserving the logarithmic qubit advantage, the authors deliver a practical encoding upgrade that boosts benchmark classification accuracy by 21–44 % over both standard amplitude and angle encodings. The result is a timely advance for near‑term QNN implementations, showing that smarter data preparation can extract far more performance from limited quantum hardware without adding trainable complexity.

Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) offer a framework for learning functions from classical data, but their expressive power depends critically on how inputs are encoded into quantum states. Angle encoding can require resources that scale with the number of features, whereas amplitude encoding represents $d$ features using only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2 d)$ qubits. This compactness comes at a representational cost: normalization makes conventional amplitude encoding invariant to nonzero real rescaling of the input, up to an unobservable global phase. We show that this invariance induces an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the resulting hypothesis class. No downstream quantum circuit can distinguish inputs differing by nonzero real scaling. We develop a general condition under which deterministic preprocessing can remove this ambiguity and show that nonlinearity alone is insufficient. Based on this analysis, we introduce a fixed nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs under subsequent amplitude encoding, without adding trainable parameters and while retaining logarithmic qubit scaling. We evaluate the resulting QNN on three canonical classification benchmarks and a nonlinear synthetic dataset against conventional amplitude and angle encoding, as well as a classical neural network. Across these tasks, the proposed encoding consistently improves classification accuracy over both quantum encoding baselines by 21$-$44 %. Our results establish normalization-induced scale invariance as a concrete representational bottleneck of amplitude encoding and demonstrate that it can be removed while preserving a compact quantum representation, marking a step toward quantum models capable of capturing arbitrary relationships in classical data.
